notes.b: Every piece of geographical information comes either from first-hand collection or from material someone else has already gathered. Textual sources are written secondary sources, so you need to know where they sit.
points: Primary data is information the student collects first-hand, such as measurements, observations, questionnaires (written sets of questions given to people), counts, field sketches and the student's own photographs.
Secondary data is information already collected or published by someone else, so the student did not gather it personally.
A questionnaire the student designs and carries out is primary, because the student collected the answers; a published survey is secondary, because someone else did.
Old maps and the census (the official count of the population) are secondary sources.
Secondary sources give background, past data and comparisons that fieldwork cannot provide, so being secondary does not make them less useful.

In the geographical investigation (the student's own research project), secondary sources supply the background and the published studies used for comparison in the conclusion. There is more on this in The Geographical Investigation (20%).
notes.tip: If asked to classify a source, a questionnaire you design and carry out is primary and a published survey is secondary. Old maps and the census are secondary. Never say secondary sources are less useful: they give background, past data and comparisons that fieldwork cannot.

notes.b: Textual and secondary sources come in many forms. Present-day ones are the ones a student can find and use now.
points: Textbooks and reference books, which give established background knowledge on a topic.
Newspapers and magazines, which report current events and issues.
Official statistics and reports from state bodies (government organisations), such as census reports, weather and climate records and environmental reports.
Local authority documents (those of the county or city council), such as county or city development plans and planning notices.
Tourist brochures and guides.
Websites and online databases.
Academic articles, which are written by researchers and scholars.
Current maps, aerial photographs (photographs taken from the air) and satellite images (pictures taken from space).

notes.h: Who produces official data in Ireland
notes.b: Official data comes from named state bodies, and knowing which body produces which kind of data tells you where to look and how far to trust it.
points: Central Statistics Office (CSO): conducts the census and publishes official statistics.
Met Éireann: the Irish national meteorological service (the body that forecasts and records the weather), which supplies weather data.
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): reports on environmental quality, including water and air.
Tailte Éireann: now responsible for national mapping. Ordnance Survey Ireland became part of it in 2023, and it now publishes the Ordnance Survey (OS) maps.
Local authorities: publish development plans, which set out how land in the county or city is to be used.
notes.tip: Match each body to its job: CSO for the census and statistics, Met Éireann for weather, EPA for water and air quality, Tailte Éireann for OS maps, local authorities for development plans.

notes.h: Past sources and change over time
notes.b: Comparing an old source with a present-day one shows change in land use, settlement, transport, the coastline or a river course. This is why sources from the past matter.
points: Sources from the past include historical maps (earlier editions of OS maps, old town plans, estate maps), old photographs and postcards, old newspapers and earlier census returns.
Other past sources include local histories, parish and school records, directories (lists of residents and businesses), travel accounts and archive documents in libraries and county archives.
The first Ordnance Survey of Ireland mapped the whole country at six inches to one mile in the 1830s and 1840s, so it gives a record of the country from that time.
Early and later map editions show field patterns, town plans, mills, demesnes (the grounds of large estates), railways and features since lost.
Old maps may use different scales, symbols and place-name spellings, and can be inaccurate or out of date, so state these limits when using them.
notes.tip: Do not treat an old map as fully accurate. Say that it may be inaccurate or out of date, and that its scale, symbols and spellings may differ.

notes.h: Comparing an old map with a present-day map
notes.b: To show change you compare the two maps in a set order. Following the steps keeps the comparison fair and lets you explain what you find.
points: 1. Match the scale and orientation of the two maps, so that distances and directions on one can be compared with the other.
2. Find fixed points, such as a bridge, church, castle or main street, that appear on both, because they let you line the maps up.
3. List what has appeared, what has disappeared and what has stayed the same.

4. Describe the change, e.g. growth along approach roads, a new bypass (a road built to take traffic around a town), the loss of a mill, reclaimed land (land made from sea or marsh) or a straightened river.
5. Explain each change, saying why it happened.
Illustrative: a Rivertown map of the 1840s shows a mill and weir on the River Dallow, a market square, the castle and fields to the north.
Illustrative, today: the OS map shows the mill gone, housing estates on those northern fields, the railway and station, an industrial estate on the N99 (a national road) and the GAA pitch.
Illustrative explanations: growth after the railway arrived, suburban expansion (building on the edge of the town), and the decline of water-powered industry, which explains why the mill has gone.

notes.b: Old photographs and written accounts record how a place once looked, so they can be compared with the place today in the same way as old maps.
points: Describe what has changed between an old photograph or written account and the present day.
Note its limits: it records a single moment, a chosen viewpoint, or the writer's own view, so it may not show the whole picture.

notes.h: Sketch map of a historical map (Higher paper)
notes.b: The Higher paper can ask for a sketch map of a historical map, worth 20 marks. The method follows the OS sketch-map rules in the notes on Map interpretation.
points: Rule a frame of the same shape as the map, with a title and a north arrow.
Historical maps usually have no grid, so divide the map and the frame into a light pencil grid of equal sections. This lets you place features accurately.
Place each requested feature by its grid section, draw it in the correct position and label it.
Show and label only the features the question asks for, because extra features are not wanted.
Illustrative: an old Rivertown town plan, 20 cm × 15 cm, is to be sketched showing the River Dallow, two connecting streets drawn meeting, the market house and the church.
notes.tip: Examiners expect a ruled frame, features correctly placed and labelled, and a title. Past questions have asked for a harbour or shoreline, two connecting streets and named buildings such as a school or a court house.

notes.b: A text is only useful once you have pulled the geography out of it. Read it for the main idea, then turn it into geographical terms and usable forms.
points: Identify the main idea of the text, then pick out its facts, figures, places and dates.
Translate everyday language into geographical terms: "the town keeps spreading into the fields" describes urban sprawl (a town growing outwards over farmland).
Use the correct term in answers and reports, e.g. hinterland (the area a town serves), nucleated settlement (houses clustered around a centre) or discharge (the volume of water a river carries).
Other correct terms are prevailing wind (the direction the wind blows from most of the time) and dependency ratio (the number of dependants compared with the working-age population).
Exam stimulus texts (the extracts given on the paper) often contain the clue term, so underline it.
Take notes under headings that match the objectives, and summarise them in bullet points.
Turn figures in a text into a table or graph, and plot places named in a text on a sketch map, so the information is easier to use.
Two sources on the same place or topic may agree, disagree or cover different dates, so cross-checking with a second source, or with primary data, increases reliability.
notes.tip: Stimulus texts often contain the clue term, so underline it and then use the correct geographical term in your answer.

notes.b: A fact can be checked against a measurement, a date or a statistic. An opinion is a view or judgement. Being able to tell them apart is a key skill for evaluating a source.
points: Illustrative extract from a Rivertown community newsletter: “Traffic on Main Street has doubled since the new industrial estate opened in 2015. The council's plan for a relief road is a disaster for the town.” The date 2015 is invented.
The first sentence is a fact: it can be checked with traffic counts or council data.
The second sentence is an opinion: it is a judgement, shown by the emotive word “disaster” (a word chosen to stir feeling rather than to inform).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to distinguish fact from opinion in a passage. Say whether each statement can be checked, and point to the emotive wording that marks an opinion.

notes.h: Bias and reliability of secondary sources
notes.b: Not every source can be trusted equally. Asking who wrote it, why and with what evidence lets you judge how far to rely on it.
points: Bias: ask who wrote the source and why, since a developer's brochure, a campaign group's leaflet, a political leaflet or an advertisement may be one-sided.
Bias shows in one-sided arguments, emotive language and selective figures (only the figures that suit the writer).
Reliability checklist, author or organisation: an official body or expert is more reliable than an anonymous author.
Reliability checklist, date: is the source current, or is it a past source useful for comparison?
Reliability checklist, purpose: does it inform, persuade or sell?
Reliability checklist, evidence: are sources cited and data given?
Reliability checklist, scale and area: national figures may not apply to the local area.
Reliability checklist, agreement: does it match other sources?
notes.tip: When evaluating a source, work through the checklist: author or organisation, date, purpose, evidence, scale and area, and agreement with other sources.

notes.h: Limitations of secondary data and a worked evaluation
notes.b: Even a reliable secondary source has limits, because it was not collected for your study. Applying the checklist to an example shows how this works.
points: Limitations of secondary data: it may be out of date, collected for another purpose, not covering the exact study area, defined differently between sources or dates, or, if online, unverified.
Illustrative: an invented property developer's brochure praising a new Rivertown housing estate is written to sell, so its purpose is persuasion.
The brochure is one-sided and gives unsourced figures, so it fails the evidence check.
To judge it, check it against the county development plan and an own land-use survey (the student's own record of how land is used).

notes.b: Using someone else's work without saying so is dishonest, so every secondary source in a report must be credited.
points: List every secondary source used in a report with its author or organisation, title and date.
For online sources, also give the web address and the date accessed, because web pages can change or disappear.
Never copy text and present it as one's own.
The authenticity of the investigation is verified by the teacher and principal. There is more on this in The Geographical Investigation (20%).

notes.h: Textual sources in the written exam
notes.b: In the written exam, textual sources appear as stimulus material (items given on the paper for you to use). Questions test whether you can use them.
points: Exam questions use stimulus material: a short text, a table, a cartoon or a newspaper-style extract.
Questions ask students to extract information, identify the issue, distinguish fact from opinion, or use the information in an answer.
Method: read the question first, so you know what to look for, then underline the key terms and figures in the text, then answer using the text's evidence plus your own knowledge.
Pictures, including cartoons, are an information source: identify the message, the issue, who is shown and the viewpoint.
notes.tip: Stimulus texts, tables and cartoons appear across the paper. Pick out the information asked for, use the correct terms, and support your answer with the evidence given.

keyTerms.definition: Information the student collects first-hand, such as measurements, observations, questionnaire answers and field sketches.
Information already collected or published by someone else.
A written secondary source, such as a textbook, report, newspaper article, plan or historical document.
A statement that can be checked against a measurement, a date or a statistic.
A view or judgement that cannot be checked directly, often shown by emotive or evaluative words.
A one-sided treatment of information, usually shaped by the author's purpose or interests.
A map from an earlier date, used with a present-day map to show change over time.
A feature, such as a bridge, church or castle, that appears on two maps and is used to match them.
The text, table, cartoon or extract given in an exam question, from which the answer is drawn.

factCards.term: Primary or secondary? How to classify questionnaires, old maps and the census
factCards.definition: A questionnaire the student designs and carries out is primary; a published survey is secondary; old maps and the census are secondary. Secondary does not mean less useful: it gives background, past data and comparisons fieldwork cannot.

factCards.term: Name six present-day and five past secondary sources
factCards.definition: Present: textbooks; newspapers; official reports; development plans; tourist brochures; websites. Past: historical maps (old OS editions, town plans, estate maps); old photographs and postcards; old newspapers; earlier census returns; parish records.

factCards.term: Who produces official data in Ireland? Name five bodies and what each supplies
factCards.definition: CSO: census and official statistics; Met Éireann: weather and climate data; EPA: water and air quality reports; Tailte Éireann: national mapping and OS maps (Ordnance Survey Ireland joined it in 2023); local authorities: development plans.

factCards.term: How to spot bias in a source
factCards.definition: Ask who wrote it and why: a developer's brochure, a campaign group's leaflet, a political leaflet or an advertisement may be one-sided. Bias shows in one-sided arguments, emotive language and selective figures.

factCards.term: Reliability checklist for a secondary source: six checks
factCards.definition: Author (official body, expert or anonymous); date (current, or past for comparison); purpose (inform, persuade or sell); evidence (sources cited, data given); scale (national figures may not fit the local area); agreement with other sources.

factCards.term: Limitations of secondary data: name five
factCards.definition: It may be out of date; it was collected for another purpose; it may not cover the exact study area; definitions may differ between sources or dates; online sources may be unverified.

factCards.term: Fact vs opinion: identify each in a passage (illustrative)
factCards.definition: Illustrative newsletter: 'Traffic on Main Street has doubled since the new industrial estate opened' is a fact, checkable with traffic counts or council data; 'the relief road is a disaster for the town' is an opinion, shown by the emotive word 'disaster'.

factCards.term: Comparing an old map with a present-day map: the five steps
factCards.definition: Match scale and orientation; find fixed points on both (bridge, church, castle, main street); list what has appeared, disappeared and stayed; describe the change (e.g. a new bypass, loss of a mill, a straightened river); explain each change.

factCards.term: First Ordnance Survey of Ireland: its scale and date, and the limits of old sources
factCards.definition: It mapped the whole country at six inches to one mile in the 1830s and 1840s. Old maps may use different scales, symbols and place-name spellings and can be inaccurate; old photographs and accounts show a single moment, a chosen viewpoint or one writer's view.

factCards.term: Sketch map of a historical map (Higher, 20 marks): the method
factCards.definition: Rule a frame of the same shape. Old maps usually have no grid, so divide map and frame into a light pencil grid of equal sections; place and label only the features asked (e.g. shoreline, two streets drawn meeting, a named building); add title and north arrow.

factCards.term: Stimulus text or cartoon questions: how to answer them
factCards.definition: Read the question first; underline key terms and figures in the text; answer using the text's evidence plus your own knowledge, in correct geographical terms. For a cartoon, identify the message, the issue, who is shown and the viewpoint.

questions.prompt: An (illustrative) old town plan of Rivertown measures 20 cm by 15 cm. Describe how you would draw a sketch map of it, showing and labelling: the River Dallow; two connecting streets; the market house; the church.
questions.model: Illustrative answer. Rule a frame of the same shape as the plan. Because the plan has no grid, divide the plan and the frame into a light pencil grid of equal sections. Place each feature by its section and draw it lightly first: the River Dallow as a continuous line across the frame; two connecting streets drawn so that they meet; the market house and the church drawn as symbols in their own sections. Label each feature with its name, then add a title and a north arrow.

questions.prompt: (a) Distinguish between primary and secondary sources of information, giving one example of each. (b) Explain two ways of checking the reliability of a secondary source.
questions.model: (a) Primary sources are information the student collects first-hand, for example a questionnaire the student designs and carries out. Secondary sources are information already collected or published by someone else, for example a published census report. (b) First, check the author or organisation: an official body or an expert is more reliable than an anonymous author, and the purpose (to inform, persuade or sell) should be noted. Second, check the evidence: a reliable source cites its sources and gives the data behind its claims, so unsourced figures can be doubted.

questions.prompt: Read this (illustrative) newsletter extract: "Traffic on Main Street has doubled since the new industrial estate opened in 2015. The council's plan for a relief road is a disaster for the town." Identify one fact and one opinion and explain your choice.
questions.model: Illustrative answer. Fact: “Traffic on Main Street has doubled since the new industrial estate opened in 2015.” It can be checked against traffic counts or council data. Opinion: “The council's plan for a relief road is a disaster for the town.” It is a judgement, shown by the emotive word “disaster”, and cannot be checked directly.
